core.text: Hypothesis: move target-identity preservation from a retained row number to an immutable-key token captured from the correction checklist at selection. Commit resolves that token against the table after refresh. Available manual key-bound replay supplies this carrier; the stipulated wrong-target trace concerns the original row carrier only.

Proposed migration replay: inspect/capture K2 at 0-1, refresh at 1-2, commit at 2-3; inspect/capture K5 at 3-4, refresh at 4-5, commit at 5-6; inspect/capture K7 at 6-7, refresh at 7-8, commit at 8-9. Prediction: captured tokens survive reordering, writes are exactly K2/K5/K7, scores remain read-only, other statuses stay unchecked and final loaded snapshot is S2. Log tokens, intended and actual keys, times and final map; no successful replay is observed.

Attack the new carrier itself in a separate diagnostic replay: keep the migration schedule and binding, but after inspecting intended K7 at 6-7 deliberately replace its captured key token with K5, exploiting the equal-score boundary as a plausible capture-confusion hypothesis. No score or source key changes. Prediction: key resolution faithfully writes K5 at 8-9, leaves K7 unchecked and logs an incorrect intended-key write. This arm fails the unchanged valued outcome even if later repaired; it is an unexecuted intervention, not evidence of actual confusion.

residue.text: Hypothesis surviving migration: stable addressing protects a correctly captured intention through row movement, but cannot establish that the captured token matches intention. Score 75 cannot distinguish K5/K7. Compare attacked and intact tokens against the checklist before committing; whether this proposed check prevents capture error remains untested.

Both migration success and capture vulnerability remain synthetic hypotheses. Real binding, capture-error frequency and interruption costs are unknown; concurrent changes, deleted keys and load failures are outside scope. Neither replay establishes repeated mismatch-refresh feedback or operational reliability.

tension.account_a: Sufficiency hypothesis: committing through an immutable key is sufficient for reliable intended-target correction, including when the captured token is replaced.
tension.account_b: Intention-integrity hypothesis: immutable binding preserves its token, so correctness additionally depends on capturing the intended key accurately.
tension.prediction_a: The corrupted-token diagnostic still writes intended K7 and ends with exactly the target map; this would require identity recovery beyond merely resolving the captured K5 token.
tension.prediction_b: The intact migration writes K7; the otherwise identical corrupted-token diagnostic writes K5 and omits K7. This separates carrier stability from intention integrity; neither result is already observed.
